Sea surface KD490 validation using gridded observations from ZISSOU¶

Matchup procedure: The model and observations were matched up as follows. First, the model dataset was cropped by a small amount to make sure cells close to the boundary were removed. The model was then regridded to the observational grid using bilinear remmaping. Only grid cells with model and observational data were maintained. The following model output was used to compare with the observational values: kd490.

Baseline climatologies of sea surface KD490¶

Climatologies of model and observational sea surface KD490 are shown in the figures below. The model climatology is calculated using the years 2000-2004.

Figure 1: Annual average surface KD490 from the model (2000-2004) and observations. Data is limited to the 2nd and 98th percentile of the combined model and observational data. Arrows indicate that values can exceed the colorbar limits.

Assessing model bias for surface KD490¶

Figure 2 shows the average bias of surface KD490 simulated by the model. A positive bias indicates that the model overestimates the observation, while a negative bias indicates that the model overpredicts the observation.

The spatial average bias of surface KD490 is 0.00 m-1. Overall, the model underestimates the observations in 52.7% of the model domain.

Figure 2: Bias of surface KD490 from the model. A positive bias indicates that the model overestimates the observation. For clarity, the colorbar is limited to the 2nd and 98th percentile of the data.

Can the model reproduce seasonality of sea surface diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm?¶

The ability of the model to reproduce seasonality of sea surface KD490 was assessed by comparing the modelled and observed seasonal cycle of KD490. First, we derive a monthly climatology for the model data. Then, we calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between the modelled and observed KD490 at each grid cell.

Note: we are only assessing the ability of the model to reproduce the ability of the model to reproduce seasonal changes, not long-term trends.

Figure 3: Seasonal temporal correlation between model and observations for surface KD490. This is the Pearson correlation coefficient between climatological monthly mean values in the model and observations.

The seasonal cycles of simulated and observed KD490 are compared in Figure 4 below. This figure shows the model and observation average in each month of the year, and the differences between the two each month

Figure 4: Monthly mean surface KD490 for the model, observation and the difference between model and observations. For clarity, the maximum values are capped to the 98th percentiles. Arrows on the colorbars indicate values beyond the colorbar limits.

Can the model reproduce spatial patterns of sea surface diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm?¶

The ability of the model to reproduce spatial patterns of sea surface KD490 was assessed by comparing the modelled and observed KD490 at each grid cell. We calculated the Pearson correlation coefficient between the modelled and observed KD490 at each grid cell.

This was carried out monthly and using the annual mean in each grid cell

Regional assessment of model performance for sea surface diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm¶

We assessed the regional performance of the model by comparing the model with observations in a number of regions. The regions considered are mapped below.

Figure 5: Regions used for validation of sea surface diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm.

Time series were constructed comparing the monthly mean of the spatial average sea surface KD490 in each region. The spatial average was calculated using the mean of all grid cells within each region, accounting for grid cell area.

Figure 6: Seasonal cycle of sea surface diffuse attenuation coefficient at 490 nm for model and observations for each region. The spatial average is taken over the region.

The table below shows the average bias of sea surface KD490 in each region. The bias is calculated as the modelled value minus the observed value. A positive bias indicates that the model overestimates the observed value, while a negative bias indicates that the model underestimates the observed value.
